difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it tests one concept (orthonormal sets and bases) where each statement is settled by direct recall or a one-line example or counterexample, about 1 minute for a prepared student.
stem: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a unique set of orthonormal basis vectors

options.label: B
options.text: $\mathbb{R}^n$ does not have a unique set of orthonormal basis vectors

options.label: C
options.text: Linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are orthonormal

solution.quick: Rotating (or reflecting) an orthonormal basis gives another orthonormal basis, so $\mathbb{R}^n$ has infinitely many orthonormal bases: (A) is false and (B) is true. Orthonormal vectors are always linearly independent (dot a vanishing combination with each vector), but not conversely: $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ are independent yet not orthonormal. So (C) is false and (D) is true. Answer: **(B), (D)**.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Vectors $q_1, \dots, q_k \in \mathbb{R}^n$ are **orthonormal** if

$$
q_i \cdot q_j = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \\ 0 & i \ne j \end{cases}
$$

that is, each has length $1$ and any two are perpendicular. In matrix form, with $Q = [\,q_1 \; \cdots \; q_k\,]$, this is $Q^\top Q = I_k$.

An **orthonormal basis** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set of $n$ orthonormal vectors that spans $\mathbb{R}^n$. Equivalently, it is the set of columns of an $n \times n$ **orthogonal matrix** $Q$ ($Q^\top Q = I_n$).

steps.title: (A) and (B): orthonormal bases are not unique
steps.body:
The standard basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ is orthonormal. But in $\mathbb{R}^2$ the rotated pair

$$
u_1 = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\right), \qquad u_2 = \left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\right)
$$

is also orthonormal: $u_1 \cdot u_2 = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 0$ and $\|u_1\| = \|u_2\| = \sqrt{\tfrac12 + \tfrac12} = 1$. It is a different basis.

In general, for **any** orthogonal matrix $Q$ the columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis, and there are infinitely many such $Q$ (e.g. a rotation by any angle $\theta$). Even in $\mathbb{R}^1$, both $\{1\}$ and $\{-1\}$ are orthonormal bases.

So (A) is **false** and (B) is **true**.

steps.title: (D): orthonormal vectors are linearly independent
steps.body:
Suppose $c_1 q_1 + c_2 q_2 + \dots + c_k q_k = \mathbf{0}$. Take the dot product of both sides with $q_j$:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} c_i\,(q_i \cdot q_j) = c_j\,(q_j \cdot q_j) = c_j \cdot 1 = 0.
$$

All cross terms vanish because $q_i \cdot q_j = 0$ for $i \ne j$. Hence every $c_j = 0$, and the only vanishing combination is the trivial one. The vectors are linearly independent. (Matrix form: $Qc = 0 \Rightarrow c = Q^\top Q c = Q^\top 0 = 0$.)

So (D) is **true**. (The paper's wording omits "in" before $\mathbb{R}^n$; the intended meaning, orthonormal vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, is clear.)

steps.title: (C): independence does not imply orthonormality
steps.body:
Take $u = (1, 0)$ and $v = (1, 1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

- They are linearly independent: $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 1 \ne 0$.
- They are not orthonormal: $u \cdot v = 1 \ne 0$ and $\|v\| = \sqrt 2 \ne 1$.

Even a single vector such as $(2, 0)$ is linearly independent but not a unit vector. Gram–Schmidt can **turn** independent vectors into orthonormal ones, but independent vectors are not orthonormal in general.

So (C) is **false**.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: The implication runs one way only: orthonormal $\Rightarrow$ linearly independent, not conversely. Orthonormal bases of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are not unique. The correct statements are **(B) and (D)**.

solution.teaching:
**Three nested properties.** For a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$:

$$
\text{orthonormal} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{orthogonal and non-zero} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{linearly independent}.
$$

Neither arrow reverses. *Orthogonal* means pairwise perpendicular ($q_i \cdot q_j = 0$ for $i \ne j$). *Orthonormal* adds unit length ($\|q_i\| = 1$). *Linearly independent* means no vector is a combination of the others, which allows vectors at any angle and of any length.

**Why orthogonality forces independence.** To test independence, suppose a combination $\sum c_i q_i$ is zero and dot it with $q_j$. Orthogonality kills every term except $c_j\|q_j\|^2$, and $\|q_j\| \ne 0$, so $c_j = 0$. This "dot with $q_j$" trick is also why coordinates are easy in an orthonormal basis: $x = \sum_j (x \cdot q_j)\, q_j$.

**Why the converse fails.** Independence only rules out redundancy. The vectors $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ point in different directions, so they are independent, but they meet at $45^\circ$ and one has length $\sqrt2$. Gram–Schmidt (or QR factorisation) converts any independent set into an orthonormal set that spans the same subspace, which shows the two notions differ.

**Orthonormal bases are plentiful.** The columns of an $n \times n$ matrix $Q$ form an orthonormal basis exactly when $Q^\top Q = I$, i.e. when $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix. Every rotation and every reflection gives one, and so does any reordering or sign flip of the standard basis vectors. So for every $n \ge 1$ there are infinitely many orthonormal bases. The standard basis is only the most convenient one. PCA, for example, picks the orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of the covariance matrix rather than the standard one.

**Back to the question.** (A) claims uniqueness, which is false. (B) denies it, which is true. (C) reverses the implication, which is false. (D) states the correct direction, which is true.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: The columns of any orthogonal matrix form an orthonormal basis. For example, in $\mathbb{R}^2$ both $\{(1,0), (0,1)\}$ and $\{(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}), (-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\}$ work. The orthonormal basis is not unique.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: There are infinitely many orthonormal bases of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (rotate or reflect any one of them). Even $\mathbb{R}^1$ has two, $\{1\}$ and $\{-1\}$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ are linearly independent (determinant $1$), but $(1,0) \cdot (1,1) = 1 \ne 0$ and $\|(1,1)\| = \sqrt2$, so they are not orthonormal.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: If $\sum_i c_i q_i = 0$, dotting with $q_j$ gives $c_j = 0$ for every $j$, so orthonormal vectors are always linearly independent.

solution.shortcut: Orthonormal $\Rightarrow$ independent (one way only), and any rotation of an orthonormal basis is another orthonormal basis. Pick the two statements that match: (B) and (D).
solution.commonTrap: Treating the standard basis as *the* orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and marking (A). Another error is reading the implication backwards and marking (C): linear independence says nothing about angles or lengths.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. The blackboard-bold R with superscript n (plain "Rn" in the PDF text layer) is transcribed as $\mathbb{R}^n$. Option (D) is printed as "Orthonormal vectors ℝⁿ are linearly independent", without "in" before ℝⁿ (compare option (C), "Linearly independent vectors in ℝⁿ"). This apparent omission in the official text is kept verbatim and not corrected; the intended reading is "orthonormal vectors in ℝⁿ". None of the options ends with a full stop in the paper. The page watermark is not part of the question.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# (A)/(B): two different orthonormal bases of R^2 (columns): standard and 45-degree rotation
E = np.eye(2); t = np.pi/4
R = np.array([[np.cos(t), -np.sin(t)], [np.sin(t), np.cos(t)]])
for name, M in (("standard", E), ("rotated", R)):
    print(name, "M^T M = I:", np.allclose(M.T @ M, np.eye(2)), "rank:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(M))
print("bases differ:", not np.allclose(E, R))
# (C): (1,0),(1,1) independent but not orthonormal
u, v = np.array([1., 0.]), np.array([1., 1.])
print("(C) rank:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.column_stack([u, v])), "u.v =", u @ v, "||v|| =", np.linalg.norm(v))
# (D): random orthonormal sets (QR of random n x k) always have full column rank
bad = 0
for _ in range(2000):
    n = rng.integers(1, 8); k = rng.integers(1, n + 1)
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.standard_normal((n, k)))
    assert np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(k))
    bad += np.linalg.matrix_rank(Q) != k
print("(D) orthonormal sets lacking full rank out of 2000:", bad)
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve by an independent verifier: orthonormal bases of R^n are not unique (the columns of any orthogonal matrix form one, e.g. the standard basis and its 45-degree rotation in R^2; even R^1 has {1} and {-1}), so (A) is false and (B) true. (1,0) and (1,1) are linearly independent but not orthonormal, so (C) is false. Orthonormal vectors are linearly independent (dot a vanishing linear combination with each q_j to get c_j = 0), so (D) is true. Answer B;D, which agrees with the official key. The NumPy check confirms that the standard and rotated bases of R^2 are both orthonormal (M^T M = I, rank 2) and differ, that (1,0), (1,1) have rank 2 but dot product 1 and norm sqrt 2, and that 2000 random orthonormal sets (QR of random n x k matrices, k <= n <= 7) all have full column rank. The checkCode previously stored in this file was an unrelated alpha-beta pruning script (a copy-paste error) and was replaced. Option (D) reads 'Orthonormal vectors R^n' without 'in' in the paper; it is read as 'orthonormal vectors in R^n', which the key treats as correct.
